turns.speaker: A
turns.text: For many years, iOS developers built screens with UIKit. In UIKit, you write step-by-step instructions. Create a label. Set its text. When the data changes, find the label and update the text again. This style is called imperative programming.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: SwiftUI, introduced in twenty nineteen, uses a different approach called declarative UI. Instead of telling the system how to change the screen step by step, you describe what the screen should look like for the current data.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: For example, you might say: if the user is logged in, show a welcome message with their name. Otherwise, show a login button. That is all. You do not write code to switch between them.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: This makes SwiftUI state-driven. The state is the data that decides how the screen looks, such as a user name, a list of items or whether a toggle is on. When the state changes, SwiftUI automatically calculates what needs to change and updates the screen. This process is called view re-rendering.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: The big benefit is consistency. In imperative code, it is easy to forget to update one label, so the screen and the data no longer match. In declarative code, the screen always reflects the current state.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: There are challenges, though. Developers need to understand where state lives and how it flows through the app. Poorly organized state can cause unnecessary re-rendering and slow performance. But once the idea clicks, many developers find it hard to go back.
